children: Welcome back. The Federal Bureau of Investigation wants to hit global hacking groups before they attack, echoing the more offensive cyber approach adopted by the White House.

In a strategy brief released Wednesday, the federal law enforcement agency said it plans to "disrupt adversaries before they can act, expose them when they do, and hold them accountable wherever they hide."
Disrupting hackers is one of four tactics outlined in the brief, along with investigations, gathering evidence and intelligence, and identifying attackers' other targets.
The core mission, the agency said, is to "impose cost on cyber adversaries."

Earlier this year, the Trump administration unveiled its long-awaited national cyber strategy, which includes a similar proactive stance against attackers, citing offensive capabilities that leverage "all instruments of national power."

The Justice Department's Scam Center Strike Force, working with the Treasury Department, took down 13 Chinese-run scam compounds operated by Xinbi, a Chinese-language marketplace where vendors sell illicit services, the agency said. U.S. authorities froze roughly $52 million in cryptocurrency as part of the operations, according to the seizure warrant.

Medical equipment company AdaptHealth said hackers stole the personal and health data of more than 4.1 million people in a June cyberattack. The ShinyHunters group claimed responsibility for the incident at the Pennsylvania-based company. (Bleeping Computer)

Longtime cybersecurity professional Kevin Mandia joined Amazon's board. The company in a blog post Wednesday cited Mandia's deep public- and private-sector experience in defending complex organizations. Mandia, Amazon said, "will help inform the Board's perspective on these opportunities and challenges."
The addition brings the company's board to 12 members. Amazon is one of the relatively few large U.S. companies with a security committee at the board level.
Percentage of organizations that lack a comprehensive incident response plan, according to a survey from TransUnion and Forrester Consulting of 327 decision makers involved with incident response.

Dealing with insider threats: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency put out updated recommendations for mitigating insider threats. The new guide has fresh case studies and data about the growing problem of employees who, knowingly or not, assist in cyberattacks. CISA's last such guidance came out in 2020.

Health and fitness apps and tracking devices no longer have to notify users of data breaches. The Federal Trade Commission revoked a regulation passed during the Biden administration that said such apps fell under rules for organizations handling protected health information. (CyberScoop)

They Lost Their Money to Scammers-and Now Battle the U.S. Government to Recover It. The U.S. seized $225 million in crypto for scam victims in Operation Big Tuna. Returning the funds has proved harder. (WSJ)
